imperial.expected: Fanging is usually caused by adding manure or compost to the soil shortly before seed sowing.
imperial.proposed: Stones, compaction, fresh manure or unfinished compost can fork roots. Properly used mature compost is suitable for no-dig carrots.

value.text: Fanging is usually caused by adding manure or compost to the soil shortly before seed sowing. Fresh manure can also make carrots tough and watery. Other causes are growing carrots in stony soil or in heavy ground which has not been properly dug.
value.control: Remove stones, improve soil deeply and avoid fresh manure.

source.value: Carrots are one of the tastiest vegetables to pull fresh from the garden, with a sweetness and earthy flavour that is hard to match from shop-bought roots. They are also one of the more awkward crops to establish well: germination can be slow, seedlings are vulnerable to slugs, and the roots need deep, fine, stone-free soil if they are to grow straight and tender. Once growing, however, carrots are very rewarding, especially if sown in short successions so that roots can be lifted from early summer into autumn. Good moisture, careful thinning, and protection from carrot fly make a big difference. In lighter soils or compost-filled no-dig beds they can be excellent, but fresh manure, compacted ground, stones, drought and rough handling all tend to produce forked, tough or damaged roots.

imperial.expected: Mix seed with sand, sow into warmed soil and keep the seedbed moist.
imperial.proposed: Mix seed with sand, sow into warmed soil and keep the seedbed moist. For November–December roots, sow a short-rooted variety in August; cover with cloches from October.

source.value: For a tender crop in November and December, sow a short-rooted variety in August and cover with cloches from October.

imperial.authority: John approved A1–A7 as-is on 15 October 2026

imperial.expected: Tie cordons loosely; remove young side shoots. Take yellow lower leaves sparingly; keep healthy leaves to feed and shade fruit. Stop two leaves above the final truss at the chosen height or near season’s end. Bush and semi-determinate pruning differs.
imperial.proposed: Tie cordons loosely; remove young side shoots. Take yellow lower leaves sparingly; keep healthy leaves to feed and shade fruit. Stop two leaves above the last useful truss, often in August under unheated cover. Bush and semi-determinate pruning differs.

source.value: Stop cordons in time for the final fruit to ripen, often in August in an unheated greenhouse. Leave two leaves above the last useful truss. As autumn growth slows, reduce watering to match demand without letting roots dry out; remove finished trusses and yellow leaves.
